writeup.headline: Ward 3 ranks 29th of 50, strong on history and fast city fixes, weak on renter strain.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: A few of these numbers carry more texture than the rank alone shows. Ward 3's National Register listings rank 2nd, but that's out of only 41 wards where the measure is filled in at all, not the full 50, so it's a strong showing on an incomplete list rather than a clean citywide comparison. The landlord profit estimate ranks the ward 47th of 50, but 11 wards land within two points of each other on that measure, so the real distance between 47th and a ward ranked in the high 30s is thinner than the number implies. And the ward's menu spending spread, which measures how concentrated the ward's yearly capital budget is across its own blocks, comes from figures tied to ward boundaries that were redrawn in 2023, so some of the historical data behind that number was collected for a differently shaped ward.
writeup.summary:
Grand Boulevard, the Near South Side, Douglas and Washington Park make up Ward 3, which lands 29th out of 50 wards overall, a middle score of 44.67. The ward runs deep on history and on how fast the city answers basic requests. It holds 31 sites on the National Register of Historic Places and 35 designated Chicago Landmarks, both among the higher counts in the city, plus 33 mapped parks, good for third place. Rodent baiting requests here close in under three days on average and street light outages get fixed in under two, both close to the fastest turnaround in Chicago.

The weaker numbers point toward housing. About 85 percent of residential parcels in the ward list a taxpayer mailing address different from the property itself, the highest share of any ward in the city and a sign of heavy landlord and investor ownership over people living in homes they own. An estimated 70 percent of rent collected on rental units in the ward ends up as landlord profit rather than paying down a mortgage, near the bottom of the 50 wards. Houses of worship here also skew toward fewer religious traditions than most of the city. Ward 3 pairs a strong historic and civic record with a rental market that leans hard toward landlords.

writeup.headline: Ward 4 ranks 17th of 50, deep in landmarks, thinner on retail and school attendance.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: The landmark count that puts Ward 4 first citywide looks commanding, but the middle half of all 50 wards spans only six points on that measure, so most wards are actually bunched close together and first place doesn't mean this ward is running away from the pack. Its 2nd-place rank on menu budget use, the share of the ward's yearly capital allotment actually spent on projects in the latest full year, comes with a similar footnote. 16 wards land within two points of each other on that measure, so the real gap between 2nd and a ward ranked in the teens is thin, and the underlying figures are tied to ward boundaries that were redrawn in 2023, so earlier years counted a differently shaped ward. The count of congregations per 10,000 residents, which ranks the ward 2nd, is built from ZIP code data that doesn't follow ward lines at all, and the source itself rates that number low confidence.
writeup.summary:
Ward 4 covers Douglas, Kenwood, the Near South Side and Oakland, and ranks 17th out of 50 wards overall, a solidly above-average score of 49.76. It stands out most for density of place. It has 130 mapped landmarks and 212 mapped civic, cultural and public places, both the most of any ward in the city, plus 755 buildings surveyed in the 1983-1995 citywide inventory of historically significant pre-1940 architecture, second most citywide. The ward also sits under three quarters of a mile from Lake Michigan on average, among the closest to the lakefront of any ward.

The weaker numbers here are about retail and schools. Roughly 60 percent of the ward's licensed food stores are chain outlets rather than independents, and about 21 percent belong to one of the 100 largest retail chains nationally, both among the higher shares in the city. Close to half the ward's students at nearby schools miss 10 percent or more of school days. The ward's own capital budget is also spent in a narrow, uneven slice of its blocks rather than across the ward as a whole. Ward 4 combines one of the city's deepest landmark counts with a retail mix leaning chain-heavy and school attendance numbers that lag much of the city.

writeup.headline: Ward 17 ranks 45th of 50 overall, weighed down by six last-place city rankings.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: The 2nd-place ranking on time poverty looks like a clear win, but it comes from a model built on national survey patterns, not a local survey, and the source itself calls it low confidence. It describes what a ward like this one typically looks like, not something measured on these actual blocks. The worst-in-the-city rank on mental health providers is a real number, 0.62 providers per 10,000 residents, but 22 other wards land within two points of it. Most of the bottom of the city is bunched together here, so the ranking is sharper than the gap behind it. Civic engagement, also ranked 50th, comes from spreading census-tract data evenly across the ward. Blocks near a ward line can end up reflecting a neighboring ward's numbers more than this one's, and the source itself rates the measure low confidence.
writeup.summary:
Ward 17 covers Auburn Gresham, West Englewood, Chicago Lawn and Englewood on Chicago's South Side. It ranks 45th of 50 wards overall. A handful of its rankings sit near the top of the city. Council session attendance for the seat ranks 2nd, at 97 percent. The ward also ranks 2nd in the city for its number of mapped houses of worship, 96 in total, and 2nd for worship places per resident. A modeled estimate of time poverty, meaning residents who get under two hours of daily leisure time, ranks 2nd, at 17.7 percent. Pothole repairs average about four days, 3rd-fastest in the city, and park acreage per resident ranks 3rd.

The weaker rankings are more numerous. Ward 17 ranks last in the city, 50th of 50, on six separate measures. Those are civic engagement, the share of adults sleeping under seven hours a night, mental health providers per resident, licensed restaurants that serve liquor, chronic school absenteeism, and the share of workers who walk or bike to their job. The ward has real physical and institutional strengths, parks, churches, fast pothole repairs, sitting next to some of the roughest numbers in the city for health access, sleep, schooling and civic life.

writeup.headline: Ward 18 ranks 35th of 50, solid on housing, thin on groceries and entertainment.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: The last-place rank on grocery stores sounds decisive. But the source itself calls this measure medium confidence, and it isn't complete for every ward. Some of what looks like Ward 18 falling behind might just be the record catching up elsewhere. The 4th-place rank for spending the aldermanic capital budget looks strong next to a full 100 percent utilization, but 16 other wards land within two points of that same score. Most of the city spends nearly all of what it's allotted, so a top-four finish here is closer to keeping pace than standing out. Rent burden, also last in the city at 63 percent, comes from census-tract estimates spread evenly across the ward. That means a tract straddling the ward line could be pulling in a neighbor's numbers along with its own.
writeup.summary:
Ward 18 covers Ashburn, Auburn Gresham, West Lawn and Chicago Lawn on Chicago's Southwest Side. It ranks 35th of 50 wards overall, closer to the middle than either extreme. Its strongest marks describe the physical stock of the place. It ranks 1st in the city for owner-occupancy, measured by how often a parcel's tax bill goes to the same address as the property itself, and 1st for having the fewest licensed tobacco retailers per resident. It also ranks 3rd for the fewest demolition permits issued and 3rd for the least residential parking-zone congestion. The ward fully spent its roughly $1.5 million annual aldermanic capital budget in the latest full year, good for 4th in the city, and ground-level sun access ranks 5th.

The weak spots cluster around retail and daily amenities. Ward 18 ranks last in the city, 50th of 50, for licensed grocery stores per resident, for licensed entertainment venues such as theaters and music halls, and for coffee shops that Google reviewers rate highly. Renters are stretched thin too. Sixty-three percent of renter households spend 30 percent or more of income on rent, the worst share of any ward. Car ownership per household ranks 49th, near the bottom of the city.

writeup.headline: Ward 19 ranks 7th of 50 citywide, though several top scores rest on modeled estimates.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: Ward 19's rank of first for voter turnout is a straight count, 62 percent of registered voters cast a ballot, the highest share of any ward, tallied against the ward's current 2023 boundaries rather than the different-shaped ward that existed in earlier elections. Its rank of 50th, dead last, on menu spending diversity looks damning next to that, but the caveat attached to the measure says the opposite: it only tracks how spread out the aldermanic infrastructure budget is across project types, and the source itself notes that concentrating money in one category isn't better or worse than spreading it around. A rank of 49th on entertainment venues carries a similar warning: 16 other wards land within two points of this ward's score, and the whole city is bunched into a 10-point range on this measure, so a rank in the high 40s reflects a small gap in a crowded field, not real distance from the middle of the pack.
writeup.summary:
Ward 19 covers Beverly, Mount Greenwood, Morgan Park and Auburn Gresham on the far southwest side. It ranks 7th of 50 wards overall, one of the higher scores in the report. The strongest numbers include the lowest measured proximity to hazardous-waste facilities of any ward, the highest share of aldermanic menu money spent on street resurfacing (99.6 percent), and the highest voter turnout in the city (62 percent of registered voters). A separate set of top scores comes from modeled estimates of resident satisfaction and safety rather than an actual local survey.

The weaker numbers describe a different kind of place. Ward 19 has the fewest grocery stores per resident of any ward, just over one per 10,000 people, and ranks near the bottom for licensed entertainment venues, fine-particulate air pollution, ride-share spending, and the share of workers who commute by public transit (9.2 percent, third lowest in the city). Together, the numbers describe a mostly residential part of the city built more around driving than transit or retail.

writeup.headline: Ward 20 ranks 46th of 50, and its poverty rate is the highest of any Chicago ward.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: Ward 20's worst score, a rank of 50th on poverty rate at 34.7 percent, comes from an actual Census count reallocated from tract data to ward lines, not an estimate, though the source rates that reallocation only medium confidence since census tracts don't line up neatly with ward boundaries. Three other bottom-ranked measures, happiness, financial satisfaction, and social trust, are modeled figures built from national survey patterns and the ward's demographic makeup rather than a poll of anyone who lives here, and the source itself rates all three low confidence. The ward's fifth-place rank on permit-zone parking density is a different case, a measure with no caveats attached at all, about as close as this report gets to a number that means exactly what it says.
writeup.summary:
Ward 20 covers New City, Washington Park, Woodlawn and Englewood on the South Side. It ranks 46th of 50 wards overall. The clearest weak point is poverty. At 34.7 percent, the share of residents living below the poverty line is the highest of any ward in the city, and median household income also ranks near the bottom, at about $40,500 a year. A cluster of modeled wellbeing measures, happiness, financial satisfaction, and social trust, land at or near last place too, though those come from estimates built on population characteristics rather than a survey of the people who actually live here.

The ward's other rankings look different. It places in the top 10 of 50 wards on the share of menu money spent on street resurfacing, on how many residential parking permit zones cover its blocks, and on new residential building permits, 22 issued over the past year. Together, the numbers point to a ward carrying real material hardship on one side and steady infrastructure and construction activity on the other.

writeup.headline: Ward 31 ranks 37th of 50, cleanest industrial-site record, weak on new housing.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: Take the No. 1 ranking on polluted-site proximity. It sounds like a clean sweep, but the source itself rates this measure only medium confidence, and it isn't filled in for every ward, so the comparison behind rank 1 is thinner than a full field of 50. The bottom-of-the-list new-housing numbers deserve the same caution in the other direction. Ward 31 ranks 50th on new homes permitted, but 29 other wards score within two points of it on that same measure, and the whole city's middle half spans under five points on it, so most of Chicago sits bunched near the bottom here too. The menu-spending rankings carry a different kind of asterisk. They're tied to today's ward boundaries, which were redrawn in 2023, so some of the historical spending data behind the 5th-place ranking on spending spread and the 6th-place ranking on sidewalk spending was actually collected for a differently shaped ward.
writeup.summary:
Ward 31 covers Belmont Cragin, Hermosa, Portage Park and Avondale on the city's Northwest Side. It ranks 37th out of 50 wards overall, a score of 36.09 that puts it in the lower half of the city. The ward's strongest numbers are environmental and civic. It has the least proximity to Superfund, brownfield and state-remediation sites of any ward in Chicago, and 71.7 percent of households here speak a language other than English at home, the fourth-highest share in the city. City services also move fast here. A street light outage gets fixed in an average of 1.68 days, one of the quickest turnarounds in Chicago, and the ward's aldermanic menu money is spent in a way that reaches a wide, even spread of blocks instead of concentrating in one corner.

The weak points cluster around housing and health coverage. An estimated 18.3 percent of residents here have no health insurance, the highest uninsured rate of any ward in the city. Parking complaints and disputes also run higher here than anywhere else in Chicago, and the city recorded only one new residential construction permit in the ward last year, the fewest of any ward. Rodent baiting requests take the longest to close of any ward too. The numbers describe a ward with clean industrial-site exposure and fast city response on basic requests, next to a housing supply that has nearly stopped growing and a bigger share of uninsured residents than anywhere else in Chicago.

writeup.headline: Ward 32 ranks 2nd of 50, strongest on income, weakest on neighbor socializing.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: A few of these rankings need the fine print attached. The modeled happiness ranking, for instance, is a statistical estimate built from the ward's income, marital status, employment, homeownership and health mix. The source rates it low confidence, so it describes what a ward with this demographic profile usually looks like more than how residents here actually feel day to day. The bars-and-taverns ranking has a different limitation. It comes from ZIP code data that doesn't follow ward lines at all, so some of what counts toward Ward 32's rank of 1st may actually sit in a neighboring ward, or miss a bar just across a ZIP boundary. The ward's near-bottom finish on mapped landmarks looks worse than the gap behind it. Twenty other wards score within two points of Ward 32 here, and the whole city's middle half spans only 6.2 points on this measure, so a landmark count drawn from OpenStreetMap is bunching most of the city together near the bottom, not singling out Ward 32.
writeup.summary:
Ward 32 covers Logan Square, Lincoln Park, North Center and Lake View on the North Side, and it ranks 2nd out of 50 Chicago wards overall, a score of 63.81. Income and material comfort drive that ranking. Median household income here is $166,248, the highest of any ward, and the poverty rate sits at 5.9 percent, the lowest in the city. A model built from income, employment, marital status, homeownership and health also puts this ward first on subjective happiness and on the modeled share of adults who would call themselves very happy. The ward also has the most bars and taverns per resident in Chicago and ranks first on a population-vulnerability score, one piece of the city's environmental justice index built from socioeconomic and health risk factors.

The weaker numbers point to time and social connection more than money. A model of daily routines puts Ward 32 last in the city on both minutes of daily leisure and the modeled share of adults who socialize with neighbors weekly, and it ranks near the bottom on time poverty too. The ward also recorded 38 demolition permits, the most of any ward, and this dataset's map of landmarks and community gardens turns up none in Ward 32, ranking near the very bottom on both. Ward 32 is a wealthy, busy ward. Residents here report less unstructured time and fewer casual neighborhood ties than people in the rest of the city.

writeup.summary:
Ward 33 covers Albany Park, Irving Park, Avondale, and North Park on the city's northwest side. It ranks 25th out of 50 wards overall, squarely in the middle of the pack. Its strongest marks come from neighborhood life rather than city government. The ward's bars carry a median Google rating of 4.75, the best score among the 45 wards with rated bars, and its houses of worship rate close behind at 4.9. Places across the ward rate second-best citywide overall, at 4.73 out of 5. Licensed food stores here skew independent more than in any other ward, with chain outlets making up just under 14 percent of the total. The ward also reports fewer traffic-crash injuries than all but two others citywide, and ranks third for how many home languages are spoken there, a mark of Albany Park's long history as a landing spot for immigrant and refugee families.

The weak points are almost all city services, not neighborhood character. Ward 33 ranks 48th of 50 on both 311 response time and pothole repair time, and dead last, 50th of 50, on the share of its yearly menu money actually spent on projects rather than left idle. The ward has no libraries mapped inside its boundaries, also last in the city. Registered murals and total place reviews rank near the bottom too, 48th of 49 and 49th of 50. The numbers describe a ward with an active bar and worship scene and mostly independent local businesses, sitting behind most of the city on infrastructure and how fast basic requests get handled.

writeup.headline: Ward 34 ranks 8th of 50, a dense downtown ward with the city's highest rent burden.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: A couple of these numbers need their caveats attached to make sense. Ward 34's last-place finish on landlord profit share, above 69 percent under both the assessed-value and sale-price versions of the estimate, looks like an outlier, but ten wards score within two points of it on each version. The ranking there is sharper than the real gap, so Ward 34 sits at the extreme end of a citywide pattern rather than standing alone. The sale-price version in particular is flagged by its own source as likely to read thin or even negative for anyone who bought recently, since it swaps in a mortgage basis closer to what current owners actually paid. On the strong side, the first-place rankings for bank branches, coffee shops, and gyms per resident come from a source that spreads county-level business counts across ZIP codes rather than ward lines, and the source itself rates that method low confidence, so a true ward-by-ward count could look different.
writeup.summary:
Ward 34 covers the Loop, Near West Side, Near South Side, and West Town, the dense center of downtown Chicago. It ranks 8th out of 50 wards overall, near the top citywide. Every one of its strongest scores comes in first in the city. It has more bank branches per resident than any other ward, at nearly 24 per 10,000 residents, and it also leads the city on coffee shops, gyms, and religious congregations, each counted per resident. It has the most 'L' station entries of any ward with rail service too, more than 7.4 million rides recorded at stations inside the ward. Licensed coffee and tea shops per resident rank first as well. The numbers describe a ward built around density and heavy daytime foot traffic more than a typical residential neighborhood.

The weak points cluster around cost of living rather than city services. Ward 34 ranks last in the city on the estimated share of rent that ends up as landlord profit, above 69 percent whether the estimate uses assessed property values or actual recent sale prices. It also ranks last on a modeled estimate of the share of adults with no religious affiliation, on licensed tobacco retailers per resident, and on the share of licensed food stores that belong to a major national chain. None of Ward 34's six weakest measures are 311 response time, pothole repair, or library and park counts, the city-service categories that show up at the bottom in many other wards.

writeup.headline: Ward 35 ranks 14th of 50, strong on restaurants and transit funding, weak on parks.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: Two of these rankings are softer than the raw numbers suggest. Park Access lands at 48th out of 50, but twelve other wards score within two points of it, and the whole middle half of the city is squeezed into an 11-point band on this measure, so the real distance between Ward 35 and much of Chicago is smaller than 48th place implies. The 4th place rank on menu money spent on bike and pedestrian projects is tied to the ward's boundaries as they stand today. Since those boundaries were redrawn in 2023, this number can't be read as a multi-year trend for one ward, only as this year's spending inside today's lines. And the ward's 46th place council attendance score blends more than one alderman's tenure across that same boundary change, on a measure the source itself rates only medium confidence.
writeup.summary:
Ward 35 covers Avondale, Logan Square, Irving Park, and Hermosa on the Northwest Side. It ranks 14th out of 50 wards overall, with a score of 51.1 out of 100. Its restaurants are mostly independent rather than chains, the second lowest chain share of any ward in the city, and its bars post some of the highest average ratings anywhere in Chicago. City infrastructure money backs that pattern up. The ward has put a larger share of its aldermanic menu funds into bike lanes, sidewalks, and street redesigns than nearly every other ward, and it spreads that money across more different kinds of projects than most wards do.

The ward falls behind on green space and a couple of slower-moving city services. Park acreage per resident is among the lowest in Chicago, and rodent baiting requests here take longer to close than in nearly every other ward. Estimated adult loneliness runs higher than most of the city too, and the ward's dense permit parking zones point to a real parking squeeze. Council attendance tied to the ward's representation lands in the bottom five, though that figure blends more than one alderman's term across the 2023 boundary change. Put together, this looks like a walkable part of the city with a strong restaurant and bar scene and real money going into biking and walking routes, though green space and a couple of routine services haven't kept up.

writeup.summary:
Ward 36 runs across Belmont Cragin, West Town, Montclare, and Humboldt Park on Chicago's Northwest Side. It ranks 27th out of 50 wards overall, with a score of 45.79 out of 100. Two of its top scores are about city government activity. The ward ranks 1st of 50 on bills sponsored, a count of non-routine legislation tied to this council session, and 1st on the share of infrastructure menu money spent on alley repair. Its houses of worship post some of the highest ratings in the city, and its bars score nearly as well as Ward 35's next door.

The weaker numbers cluster around green space, health access, and street level friction. Park acreage per resident ranks near the bottom of the city, mental health providers per resident are scarce compared to most wards, and parking complaints run higher here than almost anywhere else. Demolition permits and mapped landmarks also land in the bottom 10. The overall picture is a dense part of the city with strong food, drink, and worship options and an active council presence, alongside real gaps in park space and mental health access.
